steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Minimalism uses repetitive patterns that change GRADUALLY — tiny alterations accumulate into significant musical transformation over time.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Reich's phase shifting involves identical patterns starting together then gradually moving out of sync — creating complex textures from simple material.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Minimalist harmony often centres on a single chord or slow-moving progression — harmonic stasis focuses attention on rhythm, texture and timbre.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Technology enabled minimalist techniques: Reich's tape loops, Riley's keyboard delays, Adams' digital processing all expand what is possible with repetition.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe how minimalist music are used in a piece of music you have studied. Use musical vocabulary. | Compare how two different pieces use minimalist music. Explain the effect in each case. | How could you use minimalist music in your own composition or performance? Explain your choices.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A detailed description using precise musical vocabulary (e.g. specific terms from the AQA elements list), referencing a named piece with accurate observations about how the elements are used and their | A comparison of two pieces identifying similarities and differences in how minimalist music are used, explaining the different effects created in each musical context, using comparative language. | A practical application showing understanding of how minimalist music can be manipulated in composition or performance, with specific examples of choices made and their intended effect.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always use PRECISE musical vocabulary — not vague descriptions like it sounds nice Reference SPECIFIC musical elements when analysing any piece For listening questions: identify elements FIRST, then explain their effect For study pieces: know the context, structure and key features in detail For performing: focus on accuracy, expression and interpretation For composing: show development of ideas, not just repetition
